findings.title: Cleanup ticker interval reduced from 10 minutes to 1 minute, unrelated to stated PR scope
findings.body: The background cleanup ticker interval was changed from `time.Minute * 10` to `time.Minute * 1`. This change is not mentioned anywhere in the PR description (which is only about splitting the annotation cleanup query to avoid MySQL deadlocks) and affects *all* cleanup jobs (snapshots, dashboard versions, images, annotations, user invites, short URLs, query history), not just annotation cleanup. Running all of these jobs 10x more frequently significantly increases database load and lock contention, which directly works against the stated goal of reducing deadlocks/contention on the annotation tables. This looks like an accidental leftover from debugging/testing and should be reverted to the original 10 minute interval (or justified explicitly) before merge.

findings.title: Misuse of Error log level for routine, successful cleanup progress
findings.body: Lines 534, 537, 554, 557, 576 and 579 all call `r.log.Error(...)` to log normal, successful progress of the batched cleanup loop (e.g. "Annotations to clean by time", "cleaned annotations by time"), even when `err`/`y` is nil. These calls execute on every batch iteration (potentially thousands of times per cleanup cycle, especially combined with a now much more frequent 1-minute ticker in cleanup.go). Logging routine success at Error level will pollute error logs/alerting dashboards with false positives and generate excessive log volume (each call also logs the full `ids` slice, which can be as large as the configured batch size, e.g. tens of thousands of entries). These should be logged at Debug level and only actual failures logged as errors.

findings.title: Splitting fetch-then-delete-by-ID can delete rows that no longer match the cleanup criteria (potential over-deletion)
findings.body: CleanAnnotations/CleanOrphanedAnnotationTags now fetch a batch of IDs matching the cleanup WHERE clause in one DB session/transaction (fetchIDs), then delete strictly by those IDs in a separate, later DB session/transaction (deleteByIDs). Between the two round-trips, a row that matched the original condition (e.g. an annotation older than the cutoff, or one past the max-count threshold) could be concurrently updated (e.g. via Update(), which changes `epoch`/`epoch_end`/`updated`) so that it no longer satisfies the cleanup criteria, yet it will still be deleted because deleteByIDs only filters on `id IN (...)` without re-validating the original condition. This is the opposite of the under-deletion risk called out in the code comment ("This may under-delete when concurrent inserts happen") — in fact it can over-delete rows that were concurrently modified out of the cleanup scope, which is a data-integrity regression relative to the original single-statement subquery approach that evaluated the condition and deletion atomically.

findings.title: Raw integer concatenation into SQL string instead of parameterized query for SQLite large-batch delete
findings.body: In deleteByIDs, when running on SQLite with a batch size greater than the SQLite parameter limit (999), IDs are concatenated directly into the SQL string via fmt.Sprint/fmt.Sprintf instead of using bound parameters, unlike the normal placeholder path used otherwise. Although the values originate from fetchIDs (trusted int64 database IDs) rather than external user input, this pattern departs from parameterized-query best practice used elsewhere in the same function and is worth tightening (e.g. chunking into sub-batches of <=999 parameterized placeholders) to avoid any future risk if this code path is ever reused with less-trusted input.
